I traded in my ps3 and games for a ps4 knowing it wasn't and probably never will be backwards compatible. If they can somehow make it backward compatible in the future I will love Sony even more.

I honestly don't see how it can be so challenging. Even if it was they saw how people with xbones frothed at the mouth when they announced it. I think they'd be foolish not to as well.

In this instance it would be extremely challenging. The ps3 operating system lost a lot of similarities to windows structure, which would make emulating it on the ps4, which returned to a more standardized system pretty difficult. As well as the different engine, and the general difficulty of emulation, even on machines that are vastly more powerful, there's a lot of factors that lead complications. The answer will likely be an attempt at emulation, but the ps4 might not be powerful enough to do that efficiently. I'd be surprised if anything more than psn games were made available

Even porting PS3 games to PS4 is difficult (e.g. The Last of Us) and so with the current PS4 architecture being so different from the PS3's with its Cell processor I don't think the massive effort required would be worth it at this time. Perhaps in the future they could solve the problem by having dedicated backward compatibility hardware, but by then people won't be so attracted to PS3 titles once the PS4's library matures.

Yes, but they do offer PS2 classics on the store for the PS3.(which isn't backwards compatible except for the first run). It seems like they solved part of the problem sans hardware. Plus isn't the PS4 stronger than the XBone? Sure Cell processor and all, but a lot of these games were cross platform and ran on middleware.

I don't think it's a hardware issue, but more so of "is it going to make money". I think sony views backwards compatibility as something that only appeals to a niche audience. They are probably making more money with HD re-releases.

It definitely is a hardware issue. Emulating a whole hardware architecture in software takes a considerable amount of computing power, not to mention that writing a full emulator is a huge undertaking. We've only had a decently working PS2 emulator on PC since ~2010, and even then it took powerful hardware to run. The PS3 has had a PS2 emulator since 2011 (first PS2 Classics game was released in October 2011), which is impressive considering the PS3 is 2006 era hardware. But you have to take into account that the PS3 was powerful hardware when released and even when it was sold at a loss it cost $500-$600. And if there's someone with enough knowledge about the hardware to write a working PS2 emulator for the PS3 it's Sony, since they made both consoles. And besides that, the emulator isn't meant to run all PS2 games at 100% accuracy, it only needs to run the games available as PS2 Classics. There are probably game-specific hacks to get some games working at acceptable speeds.

I'd estimate we're still 5-7 years away from running 3D PS3 games on PC, both in hardware power and software maturity. There's already a PS3 emulator called RPCS3 but it can do only basic 2D and that's it.

I'm not sure what being cross-platform and running on middleware have to do with emulation. But as for being available on multiple platforms from a programming standpoint, it's not like they wrote the game once, compiled the code for different platforms and tadaa, the game worked everywhere. Even if developers use 3rd party game engine that's available for multiple platforms they still need to write platform-specific code to get the game running properly.

Regarding cross-platform, my understanding was that developers coded to an API that was platform agnostic, and the underlying engine was coded for each platform. Weren't there a lot of games that didn't take advantage of the Cell processor because they needed the game to also work for 360, or because the Cell processor was too difficult to work with? If the underlying API can be emulated on one platform, then why not the other? I understand there's more that goes into it that just hitting "compile and go". If I understand what MSFT is doing, they are just recompiling the software to run on the newer hardware. Emulation on the PC has always been years behind regardless of hardware.

I see what you mean but I cannot agree fully with you. As pointed out by @prepare_your_anii without dedicated hardware a software emulation would require a lot of computing power. The first PS3s solved the problem by including PS2 chips.

However, I agree with you when you say this is a question about what is going to make money. Sony has limited resources and must decide whether it's worth it to offer backwards compatibility or some other product/service. Backwards compatibility requires much developer time and dedicated hardware. In this case you mentioned HD re-releases as a direction they would prefer.
